It's broadly MECE — market attractiveness, competitive position, economics, and entry mode don't overlap much, though I'd concede access/pricing sits across buckets one and three, so I'd fold gross-to-net pricing into sizing and keep bucket three purely cost-side.

I'd prioritize bucket one, sizing. The board has set a hard gate at $300 million peak sales. If the realistic peak is below that, the competitive and entry-mode work is moot, so it's the fastest path to a yes/no. Competition is a close second because it drives the share assumption inside the sizing, so in practice I'd run them together: size the treated population, then use competitive differentiation to set peak share.

Could I get the funnel — US prevalence, diagnosed, treated — plus net price per patient-year? And if you have it, how the treated population has trended since 2022.

candidateText:
Yes, please share the forecast peak share — that's the number I need.

Ahead of it, my read: Kelvexa is a once-daily oral versus an injection every two weeks, at $8,000 net against Nimbrel's $9,000. So we're cheaper and more convenient, which is a genuine wedge in an entrenched, single-incumbent market. The offset is that Nimbrel has eight years of clinical evidence and prescriber habit, so switching existing patients is slow — most of our early volume likely comes from newly eligible or newly escalating patients rather than switches.

If the forecast peak share comes in below 18%, the board's bar isn't cleared on base economics and the question becomes whether price or eligible population can be stretched. If it's above, we're through and the conversation moves to entry mode.

One thing I'd also want: how the eligible pool has grown year over year — a growing pool makes the share hurdle easier over time.
said: Got it. Aldermoor's forecast is that Kelvexa reaches 20% of eligible patients at peak, about five years after launch. Year-over-year growth in the eligible pool — that's not something I have. Given that forecast, is the board's bar cleared on base economics, and what would you do next?

candidateText:
A few things. First, the competitive set: how many therapies are approved for moderate-to-severe Corlan's in the US, are they orals or injectables, and what share does the leader hold? If there are two entrenched biologics with 40% each, a 20% share for a new entrant is aggressive; if the category is fragmented across five products, it's more plausible.

Second, Kelvexa's differentiation — efficacy versus standard of care, safety profile, and the once-daily oral dosing, which is a real convenience advantage if competitors are injectables.

Third, and I'd weight this heavily, our own European track record. Kelvexa has been selling since 2022, so what share of eligible moderate-to-severe patients did it reach in Europe at the same point post-launch? That's the best available analogue.

Fourth, payer access — formulary tier and whether step therapy forces patients through a cheaper drug first.

I'd look for the European share data internally, and use prescription-audit data like IQVIA for US competitor shares. Do we have the European share curve?
said: A European analogue, a competitive set and payer access. Nimbrel, an injection given every two weeks, has been the standard advanced therapy for about eight years, most moderate-to-severe patients on an advanced therapy use it, and its net price is about $9,000 per patient per year. In clinical trials, Kelvexa's efficacy was similar to Nimbrel's, with fewer injection-site reactions and infections. US insurers usually require prior approval before covering an advanced therapy; Nimbrel is covered by most plans, and new drugs often take 12–18 months to win broad coverage. I don't have the European share curve. With what you now have on the competitor and payer side, how much confidence does it give you in the 20% share forecast, and what's your read?

candidateText:
The pull side is genuinely strong — 64% name the once-daily oral versus an injection, and that's the single biggest driver in the survey. Convenience advantages like that tend to translate into prescribing intent, so I'd read 64% of specialists as willing to write Kelvexa.

But the barriers bite into that. The two big ones are insurance coverage and prior approval at 58%, and no local support at 41%. Coverage is the binding one: if 58% of specialists hit prior-authorization friction, then realistically only about 42% of prescribing intent converts. So 64% × 42% ≈ 27% of specialists actively prescribing — which is still above the 20% forecast.

So the forecast looks defensible, with one condition: the 41% naming absence of local support is a problem Aldermoor creates for itself by having no US operations. That's directly fixable and it feeds straight into the entry-mode question.

Do we have data on what share of US patients sit with payers that require prior authorization?
said: Mm-hm. US insurers usually require prior approval before covering an advanced therapy; Nimbrel is covered by most plans, and new drugs often take 12–18 months to win broad coverage. Before you lean on that 27%: the survey says each specialist could pick up to two answers, and these are percentages of specialists. Walk me through why multiplying 64% by the share not naming the coverage barrier gives the share who actively prescribe.

candidateText:
Fair challenge — 12% was illustrative, not calculated. Let me build it properly.

Take the 20% forecast as the ceiling if access and infrastructure are solved. Then apply two haircuts.

Access: 58% name prior authorization as a barrier. If Nimbrel step-through applies to, say, half of covered lives in year five, those patients must fail Nimbrel first, and most who are stable on Nimbrel never move. Even if a third of that blocked group eventually reaches us, we lose roughly a quarter of the ceiling — 20% to about 15%.

Infrastructure: 41% cite no local support. Specialty drugs need reps and nurse educators for prior-auth paperwork and onboarding. With no US field force, I'd haircut another few points, to roughly 12–13%.

12% of 200,000 is 24,000 patients × $8,000 = $192 million. Well short of $300M.

But both haircuts are spend-addressable. The question isn't whether the market clears the bar — it's whether Aldermoor can build or buy the access and field capability to realize the 20%. That's the real entry question.

Do we have anything on comparable US field force costs, or whether a partner has approached Aldermoor?
said: Right. A haircut-based build. Now, an exhibit: US entry options for Kelvexa (peak year, about five years after launch). What do you take from those numbers?

Honestly, it cuts both ways, and I'd call the 20% achievable but not safe.

In favor: Kelvexa matches Nimbrel on efficacy with a better tolerability profile — fewer injection-site reactions and infections — and it's a once-daily pill versus an injection every two weeks. For a lifelong condition, that convenience advantage is real and it's the kind of thing that drives switching. And you said Nimbrel's net price is about $8,650 per patient per year, which is below our $8,000 — sorry, above our $8,000 net. So we're actually the cheaper option to the payer, which helps us on formulary.

Against: Nimbrel has eight years of entrenchment and most advanced-therapy patients are on it, so our growth has to come from switching stable patients, which is slow, plus new starts. And prior authorization with 12–18 months to broad coverage means peak year five is doing a lot of work — the first two years are close to dead.

My read: 20% at peak is defensible but I'd model a downside at 15%.

Three buckets. First, market size: can US Kelvexa sales plausibly clear $300 million at peak? I'd build that bottom-up — US prevalence of Corlan's disease, share diagnosed and treated, share on drugs in Kelvexa's class, the peak share Kelvexa could win, then net price per patient per year.

candidateText:
This is encouraging on the demand side but flags where the risk really sits.

On reasons to prescribe, the oral-versus-injection advantage dominates at 64% — that's exactly Kelvexa's structural edge and it's the top driver, which supports the switching thesis. Fewer side effects at 38% reinforces it. Interestingly, lower price is only 11%, so our price advantage matters less to prescribers than I was leaning on — it helps with payers, not with doctors.

On barriers, the top two are both things Aldermoor can actually influence. Insurance/prior approval at 58% lines up with the 12–18 month coverage lag — that's a market-access execution problem, not a product weakness. And "no local support from the company" at 41% is huge: Aldermoor has no US operations today, and specialists are telling us the absence of reps and nurse educators would stop them prescribing.

So the 20% is achievable on product merits, but it's gated on two executional things — securing payer coverage and putting feet on the ground. That directly informs entry mode: we can't do this with a bare-bones presence. Should I move to the recommendation?
